summary: A reply to Wayne Hathaway's RFC 513 about the Telnet SYNCH sequence. The authors agree that the phrase interesting things is too vague for a specification, but disagree that SYNCH should be redefined. They argue the problems come from higher-level protocols such as FTP misusing it.

eli5.summary: A debate about a signal that tells a computer to skip ahead. The authors say it is fine and people use it wrongly.

subtitle: Why the Telnet SYNCH sequence is fine, and why higher-level protocols should build their own.

tldr.problem: RFC 513 argued that the Telnet SYNCH sequence depends on a vague notion of "interesting things" and proposed redefining it.
tldr.mechanism: The authors keep the Telnet definition and say protocols built on Telnet, like FTP, should have their own synch: the Telnet IP as the out of band signal plus a higher-level data mark in the stream.
tldr.outcome: The difficulties come from higher-level protocols misusing Telnet SYNCH at two protocol levels, not from a Telnet flaw.

facts.label: Out of band signal for higher levels

sections.title: Agreeing and Disagreeing with RFC 513
sections.content: The authors respond to Wayne Hathaway's RFC 513. They agree that the phrase "interesting things" is too imprecise for a protocol specification. They disagree that the Telnet SYNCH definition should change, and say the difficulties reflect misuse of SYNCH by higher-level protocols, in particular FTP, rather than a Telnet design flaw.
sections.eli5: They agree one phrase was too fuzzy, but they say the rule itself is right.

sections.title: What a Synch Sequence Is
sections.content:
A synch sequence brings signals that are stuck in the pipeline to the attention of the protocol interpreter, which may be busy elsewhere. It has two parts: an "out of band" signal to get attention, and an "in band" marker showing how much of the stream to process. For Telnet, these are the Host-Host Protocol INS and the Telnet Data Mark (DM).

The "interesting" characters for Telnet are the Telnet commands, including option negotiation and sub-negotiation. A host may also treat its own terminal signals as interesting, such as ^C and ^T on TENEX. The implementer must interpret all Telnet commands and may ignore or pass on the extra signals, so there is no vagueness for him.
sections.eli5: A synch is a tap on the shoulder plus a marker in the line that says how far to read.

sections.title: Synch for Protocols Built on Telnet
sections.content:
The vagueness appears when a higher-level protocol uses Telnet SYNCH to push its own commands through. A Telnet interpreter cannot know which things are interesting to the protocol above it, and should not have to, just as an NCP should not have to know what kind of connection it carries. Giving SYNCH meaning at two protocol levels violates protocol layering.

The proposed fix is for the higher-level protocol to define its own synch: insert the Telnet IP as the out of band signal, then place a higher-level data mark (HDM) after the commands that matter. The receiver is interrupted and scans up to the HDM.
sections.eli5: Each program should use its own tap-and-marker, not borrow Telnet's.

sections.title: Example: Aborting an FTP Transfer
sections.content:
To abort a transfer, the FTP user sends the Telnet IP character, then the Telnet SYNCH sequence (the DM and the Host-Host INS), then the FTP ABOR command, then the FTP data mark. The Telnet SYNCH in step two ensures the IP reaches the server's Telnet interpreter.

The endnotes add that the authors support fully parenthesizing sub-negotiations, with a new command as the closing parenthesis rather than a second SB. They disagree that sub-negotiations should be discarded during a SYNCH. They also say an FTP data mark is not yet defined and may be unnecessary.
sections.eli5: To stop a file copy, you tap the server, signal Telnet, say "abort", and mark the end.
